body_text: A routine journey through a forest in Indonesia ended in tragedy after a mother of four was reportedly attacked and swallowed by a huge reticulated python. The woman, identified as 50-year-old Farida, had been travelling through a forested area in Kaumpang, in West Sulawesi's Mamuju Regency, when she disappeared. She had reportedly been making her usual journey to sell food at a nearby market. Her disappearance prompted a search involving relatives, local residents and authorities. What they eventually discovered left the community horrified. According to reports, Farida was attacked by a large reticulated python, a species known for its exceptional size. The snake was later discovered with a greatly enlarged stomach, leading villagers to believe it had swallowed the missing woman. Woman disappears while travelling through forest Farida had reportedly been following a familiar route through a forested area when the incident occurred. The journey was connected to her regular work selling food at a market close to her home. Reports say the enormous snake approached her and bit her leg. The python then constricted her body, an attack that reportedly resulted in her death. Reticulated pythons are powerful constrictors. Rather than relying on venom, they use their muscular bodies to restrain prey before feeding. In Farida's case, the snake reportedly swallowed her body whole, beginning with her head. The incident only came to light after her family realised that she had not returned home. By nightfall, her husband, Noni, had become increasingly concerned. He contacted members of the local community and began searching for his wife with other villagers and authorities. The search continued until the group encountered a huge python in a wooded area. Searchers discover giant python The snake reportedly measured around 20 feet in length and had a noticeably swollen stomach. According to the report, the unusual appearance of the snake raised suspicions among the search party. Villagers eventually cut open the python and discovered Farida's body inside. The discovery brought a devastating end to the search. Reports stated that Farida was still wearing her clothes when she was found. Her remains were subsequently covered and taken away by members of the community. The shocking discovery reportedly took place in front of a large crowd of villagers, highlighting the profound impact the incident had on the local community. Farida was later given a funeral and buried in the Pitu Riawa district of Sidrap Regency. A rare but frightening type of snake attack The reticulated python, scientifically known as Malayopython reticulatus , is recognised as the longest snake species in the world. Individual snakes can reach extraordinary lengths, although most encounters with people do not end in attacks of this nature. The source article notes that a reticulated python in Indonesia holds the record for the longest wild snake ever recorded, measuring 7.22 metres. Despite their size and strength, incidents involving pythons swallowing adult humans are unusual. However, the report points to previous cases in Indonesia in which people were discovered inside large pythons after going missing. The local village head, Suardi Rosi, reportedly said that this type of danger was not something residents normally feared and that the incident was believed to be the first of its kind in that particular area. The tragedy has nevertheless drawn attention to the risks that can exist in forested and agricultural environments where people and wildlife share the same surroundings. Previous incidents have also been reported Farida's death was not the first reported case of a person being found inside a python in Indonesia. The source reports that a similar incident occurred in 2022 involving a 54-year-old woman named Jahrah. She reportedly disappeared while carrying out a harvesting errand and was found two days later inside a python. Another case was reported in 2018, when a woman named Wa Tiba, also aged 54, disappeared while checking her vegetable garden. Her sandals and machete were reportedly found in the area before villagers discovered a python with a swollen stomach. These cases remain extremely unusual, but they demonstrate why encounters between humans and very large constrictor snakes can sometimes have devastating consequences. Why reticulated pythons are so powerful Reticulated pythons are non-venomous snakes that rely on their physical strength to capture prey. Their bodies are highly muscular, allowing them to restrain animals through constriction. Their enormous length gives them a significant advantage when hunting. They can also move through forests, agricultural areas and other environments where their prey may be found. The species is native to parts of South and Southeast Asia and is particularly associated with tropical environments. Although these snakes generally avoid people, their size means that encounters can become dangerous under certain circumstances. A person travelling alone through a forest may have little warning if a large snake is hidden nearby. That does not mean attacks on humans are common. Instead, cases such as Farida's are notable precisely because they are so rare and extreme. A devastating loss for Farida's family For Farida's family, the incident was not simply a frightening wildlife story. It was the sudden loss of a wife and mother. Her husband reportedly expressed deep regret after learning what had happened. He described his sorrow over allowing his wife to travel alone and expressed concern about the suffering she may have experienced. Farida's death has also affected the wider community, where residents reportedly gathered during the search and aftermath. The circumstances surrounding her disappearance make the tragedy particularly distressing. What began as an ordinary journey to a nearby market ended with an unexpected encounter with one of the world's largest snake species. The incident serves as a reminder that people living and working close to forests can sometimes encounter wildlife capable of causing serious harm, even when such events are highly unusual. For Farida's loved ones, however, the story is ultimately about a personal loss that cannot be measured by the size of the snake or the shock surrounding the discovery. Her family and community were left to mourn a woman who had simply set out to complete part of her normal daily routine. Source A report published by the Irish Mirror on August 9, 2026. The original report attributes some details to local accounts and the Daily Mail.

title: 8 Best AI Voice Agents for Inbound & Outbound Call Centers in 2026
summary: 8 AI voice agent platforms compared on telephony, latency, compliance, and pricing for inbound and outbound call centers.
body_text: AI voice agents have moved past the “interesting demo” stage. Teams are now using them to answer inbound calls, qualify leads, book appointments, handle routine support, follow up with prospects, and hand conversations over to a human when needed. The global AI voice agents market was valued at $2.54 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $35.24 billion by 203 3, growing at a 39% CAGR, according to Grand View Research . More businesses are moving real customer conversations, not just experiments, onto AI-powered voice systems. The problem is that most platforms look pretty similar until you put them under real call volume. That’s when the differences start to show up: response delay, transfer quality, telephony setup, compliance, pricing, and how much work your team has to do to keep the agent running well. This guide compares the AI voice agent platforms worth evaluating in 2026 for both inbound and outbound call-center use cases, with a focus on what actually matters once you move from a demo into production. TL;DR Plivo is the strongest all-round option for teams that want inbound and outbound AI calling, telephony, compliance, and global coverage in one setup. Retell AI is a good fit for teams that want faster deployment without building the full voice stack themselves. Vapi and LiveKit are better suited to developer-led teams that want more control over models, telephony, and infrastructure. Bland AI stands out for high-volume outbound calling, while Synthflow AI is easier for no-code teams. ElevenLabs is worth shortlisting when natural voice quality is the main priority. Twilio makes the most sense if your communications stack already runs there. For most buyers, the real decision comes down to how much infrastructure you want to manage yourself. If you want fewer moving parts across AI and telephony, Plivo is a strong place to start. What Actually Matters When Choosing a Voice AI Agent Most voice AI comparisons focus on how natural the agent sounds or which model it uses. Those things matter, but they don’t tell you whether the platform will actually hold up once real customers, real call volume, and real compliance requirements enter the picture. 1. Telephony Ownership and Infrastructure A voice AI agent is still running on a phone network, so phone numbers, routing, carrier reliability, and geographic coverage matter just as much as the AI itself. If the platform relies on a separate telephony provider, you’re adding another system into the call path and another vendor to troubleshoot when something goes wrong. 2. End-to-End Latency A great voice model can still feel awkward if there’s too much delay between the caller finishing a sentence and the agent responding. Look at end-to-end latency across telephony, transcription, the LLM, and voice generation, not just the speed of one component. 3. Enterprise Compliance For healthcare, financial services, insurance, and other regulated industries, compliance can narrow the shortlist pretty quickly. Depending on your use case, look for things like SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR, and data residency controls, and confirm that they actually cover the voice product you plan to use. 4. Code + No-Code Builder Access The people who understand customer conversations best are often in support, sales, or operations, and they shouldn’t need an engineer every time a prompt or call flow needs changing. At the same time, developers still need APIs and deeper controls for custom integrations and more complex workflows. 5. Omnichannel Support Inbound and outbound calls are usually only one part of the customer conversation. If someone calls, then follows up over SMS, WhatsApp, or chat, carrying that context across channels can make the experience a lot smoother and reduce the amount of stitching your team has to do behind the scenes. 6. Post-Deployment Quality Tooling Getting the agent live is only the beginning. The real problems usually show up once actual customers start calling, so look for simulation testing, call evaluations, conversation scoring, and tools that help your team spot and fix recurring issues after launch. A Detailed Comparison Tool Best For Inbound + Outbound Owned Telephony Enterprise Compliance Pricing Plivo Enterprises wanting AI and telephony in one platform Yes Yes Yes $0.04/min Vapi Developer-led teams building highly customized voice agents Yes - Yes $0.05/min platform fee; realistic all-in cost ~$0.13–$0.33/min Retell AI Mid-market teams that want to deploy quickly Yes - Yes $0.07–$0.31/min for AI Voice Agents Bland AI High-volume inbound and outbound call automation Yes Yes Yes $0.14/min Synthflow AI No-code teams automating sales and support calls Yes Yes Yes Pay as you go ElevenLabs Teams prioritizing natural voice quality Yes - Yes $6/mo Twilio Enterprises already running communications on Twilio Yes Yes Yes Pay as you go LiveKit Developers building custom voice or multimodal applications Yes - Yes $50/mo Plivo Plivo is a strong fit for teams that want inbound and outbound AI calling without stitching together a separate telephony provider, voice layer, and agent platform. It combines Voice AI Agents with its own communications infrastructure, so teams can handle support calls, lead qualification, appointment booking, follow-ups, and human transfers from one setup. The bigger advantage is operational simplicity. Because telephony and the AI agent layer sit closer together, there are fewer systems to manage once call volume starts climbing. Ops teams can use the no-code builder for day-to-day changes, while developers still have APIs when they need deeper control. Key Strengths Inbound and outbound in one platform: Teams can use the same setup for customer support, lead qualification, appointment booking, follow-ups, and other call-center workflows. Telephony and AI together: Plivo combines the phone network and AI agent layer, which means fewer vendors and fewer systems to troubleshoot when something goes wrong. No-code + developer control: Ops teams can make everyday changes without relying on engineering, while developers still have APIs for more complex workflows and integrations. Built-in human handoff: Agents can transfer calls to a person when the request gets too complex or needs human judgment. Broader communication options: Plivo also supports SMS, WhatsApp, and chat, which is useful when the conversation needs to continue after the call. Limitations Less modular for teams that want to pick every provider themselves: If your developers want separate control over telephony, transcription, LLMs, and voice providers, a platform like Vapi or LiveKit may give them more flexibility. Larger deployments may need Enterprise: Higher concurrency, broader international coverage, and some enterprise controls sit beyond the standard self-serve setup. Pricing Plivo Voice AI Agents cost $0.04 per minute. The per-minute pricing generally covers the full voice AI stack, including telephony connection, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, LLM processing, and real-time agent orchestration during the call. Vapi Vapi is a better fit for developer-led teams that want to build inbound and outbound voice agents without being locked into one AI or telephony provider. You can choose your own speech-to-text model, LLM, voice provider, and phone infrastructure, then use Vapi to orchestrate the conversation between them. That flexibility is the main appeal. It gives engineering teams a lot of control over how the agent behaves and what each part of the voice stack costs, but it also means there are more pieces to configure and manage once you move into production. Key Strengths Highly modular setup: Teams can choose their own telephony, transcription, LLM, and voice providers instead of working within a fixed stack. Strong developer control: Vapi is API-first, which makes it a good fit for custom routing, internal tools, CRM integrations, and more complex inbound or outbound workflows. Inbound and outbound support: The same platform can handle customer-facing inbound calls as well as outbound use cases like qualification, follow-ups, and appointment scheduling. Flexible provider choices: Teams can swap models or voice providers as requirements around quality, latency, or cost change. Testing and evaluation tools: Vapi includes tooling for testing agent behavior before and after launch, which is useful once real conversations start surfacing edge cases. Limitations Telephony is still a separate layer: Vapi works with external telephony providers, so your setup can involve multiple vendors rather than one end-to-end platform. More engineering-heavy: The flexibility is useful, but non-technical teams may need developer help for setup, integrations, and ongoing changes. Pricing can be harder to predict: The platform fee is only one part of the cost. Telephony, transcription, LLM, and voice usage are billed separately. More moving parts to troubleshoot: If call quality drops or latency increases, finding the issue can mean checking several providers rather than one system. Pricing Vapi charges a $0.05 per minute platform fee. Once telephony, speech-to-text, LLM, and voice costs are included, a realistic all-in cost can land around $0.13 to $0.33 per minute, depending on the providers and models you choose. Retell AI Retell AI is a good fit for teams that want to get inbound and outbound voice agents live quickly without building the entire voice stack themselves. It brings agent building, telephony, transfers, testing, analytics, and monitoring into one platform, while still giving developers APIs, webhooks, and custom telephony options when workflows get more complex. Key Strengths Inbound and outbound support: The same platform can handle customer support and routing on the inbound side, plus follow-ups, qualification, and other outbound workflows. Strong transfer options: Retell supports cold and warm transfers, including private messages and three-way introductions, which makes human handoffs more useful than simply dropping a caller into another queue. Faster deployment: Agent templates, testing, telephony, analytics, and transcripts are available in the same platform, so teams have fewer pieces to assemble before going live. Flexible telephony: Teams can use Retell-managed phone numbers or connect their own telephony setup depending on what they already have in place. Useful post-call tooling: Call analytics, transcripts, simulation testing, and post-call data make it easier to see where agents are working well and where they need tuning. Limitations Telephony isn't fully owned end-to-end: Retell can manage the telephony experience, but its phone setup still relies on underlying carrier infrastructure rather than an owned global carrier network. Some features depend on your telephony setup: Certain transfer capabilities can vary depending on whether you're using Retell-managed or custom telephony. Pricing can vary quite a bit: The final per-minute rate changes based on the model, voice, and other components you choose, so the lowest advertised rate won't necessarily be your production cost. Outbound requires an extra setup step: Retell requires KYC verification before outbound calling is enabled, which is worth factoring into the rollout process. Pricing Retell AI uses pay-as-you-go pricing from $0.07 to $0.31 per minute for AI Voice Agents. The final rate depends on the model, voice, telephony setup, and other components selected for the agent. Bland AI Bland AI is a strong fit for teams running a lot of inbound or outbound calls and wanting more control over how those conversations are handled. It supports use cases like lead qualification, inbound support, appointment booking, routing, and warm transfers, with higher concurrency available as call volume grows. Key Strengths Built for high call volume: Bland supports 10 concurrent calls on Start, 50 on Build, and 100 on Scale, with custom concurrency available for Enterprise. Inbound and outbound support: The same platform can handle inbound support calls as well as outbound sales, qualification, and follow-up workflows. Strong transfer options: Bland supports live and warm transfers, which is useful when the AI needs to bring a human into the conversation without losing context. Flexible telephony setup: Teams can use Bland phone numbers or connect existing SIP and Twilio infrastructure for inbound and outbound calling. Enterprise deployment options: Larger teams can move to dedicated infrastructure, VPC or on-prem deployment, SSO, data residency, and custom concurrency. Limitations More technical than a pure no-code platform: Bland is API-first, so more complex call flows and integrations are a better fit for teams with some technical resources. Telephony setup can still involve another provider: If you bring your own SIP or Twilio setup, there are still multiple systems involved when troubleshooting call issues. Some useful features sit on higher plans: Concurrency, transfer pricing, knowledge-base limits, and enterprise controls improve as you move up the pricing tiers. High-volume deployments need closer cost planning: The per-minute price comes down on larger plans, but platform fees and transfer charges still need to be included when estimating total call-center costs. Pricing For the Start plan, you get $0.14 per minute usage, support for inbound and outbound calling, API access to build call workflows, live/warm transfer capability, and up to 10 concurrent calls. Synthflow AI Synthflow AI is a good fit for teams that want to automate inbound and outbound calls without making engineering the bottleneck. It gives operations teams a more visual way to build and manage voice agents, while still supporting existing telephony setups and more complex call-center workflows. Key Strengths Inbound and outbound support: Teams can use Synthflow for incoming support and routing as well as outbound follow-ups, qualification, and appointment booking. No-code friendly: Ops teams can build and update agents without relying on developers for every prompt, workflow, or routing change. Flexible telephony setup: Teams can use Synthflow phone numbers or connect existing Twilio, SIP, or PBX infrastructure. Good fit for call-center workflows: The platform supports routing, appointment booking, voicemail detection, transfers, and follow-up actions. Enterprise-ready options: Larger deployments can add higher concurrency, security controls, integrations, and implementation support. Limitations Less control for deeply technical teams: Developers who want to choose and manage every model, voice provider, and infrastructure component may prefer Vapi or LiveKit. Telephony setup can vary: Depending on how you deploy it, calls may still involve Twilio, SIP, or another existing phone system. Pricing becomes less straightforward at scale: Larger deployments depend on call volume, telephony, integrations, and support requirements rather than one simple rate. Some advanced controls sit behind larger plans: Enterprise security, higher concurrency, and more complex implementation requirements may need a custom agreement. Pricing Synthflow uses pay-as-you-go pricing for self-serve usage. Larger enterprise deployments move to custom pricing based on call volume, telephony setup, integrations, security requirements, and support needs. ElevenLabs ElevenLabs is a strong fit for teams where voice quality is a big part of the customer experience. ElevenAgents supports inbound and outbound calling, multilingual conversations, human transfers, and telephony integrations, making it useful for support, qualification, follow-ups, and other customer-facing call workflows. Key Strengths Natural-sounding voices: Voice quality is ElevenLabs’ biggest strength, especially for customer-facing calls where a robotic experience can hurt trust. Inbound and outbound support: Teams can use ElevenAgents for incoming support calls as well as outbound follow-ups, qualification, and campaign workflows. Multilingual conversations: The platform supports multiple languages, which makes it useful for teams serving customers across different regions. Works with existing telephony: Teams can connect existing phone systems through SIP or other telephony providers rather than replacing everything. Strong compliance coverage: ElevenLabs supports enterprise requirements including SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, GDPR, PCI DSS, and multiple ISO certifications. Limitations Telephony is still a separate layer: ElevenLabs handles the AI and voice experience, but phone connectivity can still depend on another telephony provider. Not a full contact-center platform: Teams that need deeper queue management, workforce tools, or broader contact-center operations may need additional systems. More moving parts to manage: Using separate telephony gives you flexibility, but it also means more systems to configure and troubleshoot. Voice quality may not be the main priority for every team: If telephony ownership, routing simplicity, or infrastructure consolidation matter more, another platform may be a better fit. Pricing ElevenLabs starts at $6 per month. Higher plans included usage and concurrency, while additional agent usage, LLM usage, and telephony can add to the final production cost. Twilio Twilio is a strong fit for enterprises that already run a large part of their communications stack on Twilio. It supports inbound and outbound voice workflows, gives developers control over routing and call logic, and lets teams add AI on top without replacing the telephony infrastructure they already use. Key Strengths Inbound and outbound support: Teams can use Twilio for customer support, routing, follow-ups, sales calls, and other two-way voice workflows. Own telephony infrastructure: Twilio operates the phone network, numbers, SIP, and routing layer, which removes the need for a separate carrier. Strong developer control: APIs and programmable voice tools make it a good fit for teams building custom call flows and integrations. Broad communication coverage: Twilio also supports SMS, WhatsApp, and other channels, which is useful if voice is only one part of the customer journey. Enterprise compliance: Twilio supports requirements like SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, PCI DSS, and multiple ISO certifications. Limitations Still developer-heavy: Teams usually need engineering support to build and maintain the AI logic, routing, and integrations. Not the easiest no-code option: Ops teams that want to manage agents without technical help may find Retell or Synthflow easier. Pricing comes from multiple services: Voice, AI, phone numbers, and other communication products are billed separately, so the true cost can be harder to estimate. Best fit depends on your existing setup: If you are not already using Twilio, adopting it just for AI voice can add more infrastructure than you need. Pricing Twilio uses pay-as-you-go pricing. Voice, AI, phone numbers, and other services are billed based on usage, with volume discounts available for larger deployments. LiveKit LiveKit is a good fit for developer-led teams that want to build custom inbound and outbound voice experiences rather than use a more packaged call-center platform. It gives developers the real-time media layer, telephony support, agent framework, and model flexibility needed to create highly customized voice workflows. Key Strengths Inbound and outbound support: Teams can build both incoming call flows and outbound calling workflows on the same platform. Built for real-time voice: LiveKit is designed around low-latency audio and real-time communication, which makes it well suited to conversational AI. Flexible AI stack: Developers can choose different speech-to-text, LLM, and voice providers depending on quality, latency, or cost requirements. Strong telephony support: LiveKit supports SIP, phone numbers, transfers, and traditional phone connectivity for AI agents. Multimodal by design: It can also support video and other real-time experiences, which makes it useful for teams building more than just a phone agent. Limitations Developer-first setup: LiveKit is better suited to engineering teams than ops teams looking for a simple no-code platform. More building is required: You get the components to create the experience, but routing, business logic, and integrations still need to be built around them. Telephony can involve another provider: Depending on the setup, teams may still use an external SIP or carrier provider for phone connectivity. Pricing has multiple components: Agent usage, telephony, AI models, and real-time infrastructure can all contribute to the final cost. Pricing LiveKit plans start at $50 per month. Final costs depend on agent usage, telephony, real-time media, and the AI models used in the deployment. Choo sing the Right Voice AI Agent for Your Call Center The right platform usually comes down to four things: how regulated your industry is, where your calls happen, how technical your team is, and whether you're optimizing for inbound, outbound, or both. If you're a regulated or global enterprise Plivo is one of the strongest options if you need telephony, AI agents, compliance, and international coverage in one setup. It also works well for mixed teams because ops can handle day-to-day changes through no-code tools, while developers still have APIs when they need more control. Twilio is also a strong fit if your communications stack already runs there. In that case, extending what you already have may be more practical than moving to a new platform. If you're building a custom voice AI product Vapi makes more sense if your developers want to choose the telephony provider, LLM, speech-to-text, and voice provider themselves. You get more flexibility, but you also take on more of the setup and maintenance. LiveKit is the better option if you're building something broader than phone calls, especially voice, video, or other real-time experiences. If you're a small business or agency Synthflow AI is a good place to start if ease of use matters more than deep technical control. It works well for simpler workflows like appointment booking, lead qualification, and basic support without making engineering part of every change. If outbound volume is the priority Bland AI is worth considering for sales teams or other high-volume outbound use cases. It's more geared toward large calling workflows than some of the broader voice-agent platforms. If voice quality matters most ElevenLabs stands out when the conversation needs to sound as natural as possible. It's a strong choice for customer-facing calls, but you'll still need to think about the telephony, routing, compliance, and operational layers around it. For most teams starting fresh, Plivo is a strong place to begin the shortlist because it brings telephony and AI together without forcing you to manage as many separate systems. But if you're already deeply invested in another stack, the switching cost matters just as much as the feature list. Final Thoughts Choosing an AI voice agent comes down to more than how good the demo sounds. Once the platform is handling real inbound and outbound calls, things like telephony, routing, compliance, latency, and day-to-day manageability start to matter a lot more. Vapi and LiveKit give developer-led teams more control. Synthflow is easier for no-code use cases, Bland AI is a better fit for high-volume outbound, ElevenLabs stands out on voice quality, and Twilio makes sense if you're already deep in its ecosystem. For teams starting fresh, Plivo is one of the stronger options to evaluate because it brings telephony and AI agents together in the same setup, while still giving both ops and engineering teams room to work. That can make the overall deployment simpler, especially as call volume, compliance requirements, and geographic coverage start to grow. The best move is to shortlist two or three platforms and test them on the call flows that matter most to your business. The platform that holds up under real traffic is usually the one worth scaling. Want to test a more integrated voice AI setup? If you're looking for a platform that combines inbound and outbound AI agents with telephony, compliance, and global coverage, Plivo is worth putting on the shortlist. Explore Plivo Voice AI Agents

title: What 170 Students Think of AI-Generated Instructional Videos (2026 Study)
summary: A peer-reviewed 2026 study at two US universities had 170 computing students watch AI-generated instructional videos made with Knowlify. Students rated the videos 4.52 out of 5 for production quality and scored 86% on a knowledge test, half could not tell the videos were AI-generated, and 68% still preferred videos recorded by their instructor.
body_text: Where Students Said It Does Not Belong Poor fit Students Share Complex, advanced, or nuanced topics 50 31% Subjective topics such as philosophy, ethics, art, and public speaking 22 14% Replacing instructor-led lectures entirely 26 16% Interactive learning such as debugging, algorithm design, and seminars 14 9% Niche topics with limited source material online 6 4% The boundary students drew is sharp. Complex material needs elaboration, back-and-forth, and someone who can respond to the specific shape of a student's confusion. As one student explained, discussions "require dynamic back-and-forth perspective sharing and real-time responses to student viewpoints." Nobody claimed a video could do that. What Students Are Worried About Concerns were coded from the same 163 responses. Nine students (6%) reported no concerns at all. Concern Students Share Inaccurate or hallucinated information 94 58% Lack of depth, oversimplification, skipped steps 22 13% Lack of engagement, monotone delivery, pronunciation errors 21 13% Fewer interactions with instructors and TAs 16 10% Undermines the value of tuition 17 10% Missing instructor insight and personal experience 9 6% Broader societal impacts including instructor pay and energy use 9 6% No thorough fact-checking by an educator 7 4% Cannot ask follow-up questions 6 4% Instructors may reduce effort and offload teaching 5 3% Accuracy dominates everything else. At 58%, it was named more than four times as often as the next concern. One student summarized the asymmetry neatly: "although professors can make mistakes, my experience of AI is that it will." There is a subtler concern in that table worth pulling out. Seven students noted that high production quality can itself be a risk, because a polished video can "lull a false sense of security" and make errors easier to miss. Given that this study also found students rated production quality at 4.52 and half could not detect AI generation, that warning is well placed. The better the output looks, the more the human review step matters. What This Means If You Are Building Video The study was run in a computing classroom, but the findings transfer cleanly to corporate training, customer education, and documentation. Deploy AI video where students already said it works. Foundational concepts, syntax and procedure, visual processes, summaries and refreshers, and supplemental explanations of material that also exists in writing. This maps almost exactly onto the highest-volume, lowest-differentiation content in most training video libraries and most new-hire onboarding programs . Keep a human in the loop and say so. Accuracy was the top concern by a wide margin, and four percent of students specifically worried that nobody had reviewed the video end to end. In the study itself, each video included roughly 10 minutes of human verification time. Build that step into your process and tell users it happened. Do not position AI video as a replacement for a person. The data on this is unambiguous. Comfort sits at 46% when AI video is described as instructional material and drops to 10% when it is framed as a substitute for the instructor. The framing changes the reception more than the content does. Expect the format to carry more weight than you think. The single most consequential design choice in this study was removing the avatar. Animated explainers scored 4.52 on production quality in a literature where avatar-based videos had previously been called distracting and uncanny. If your audience is skeptical, animation is the safer format. How the Videos Were Made For teams evaluating the production economics, the paper documents the workflow precisely. The researchers uploaded GitHub's official Markdown formatting documentation as a PDF to Knowlify and used a one-shot prompt to generate each video. The platform produced a narration script, a scene-level storyboard, and voiceovers, all reviewable and editable before final render. Production metric Result Planning, reviewing, and configuring 8 to 11 minutes per video System generation time 3 minutes 48 seconds average Human verification About 10 minutes per video Total time per 3-minute video At most 25 minutes Cost per video at study-period pricing Roughly $50 to $60 Twenty-five minutes of total human and machine time per finished three-minute video is the number worth holding onto. Traditional instructional video production is typically quoted per finished minute in the hundreds to thousands of dollars and measured in days or weeks. For a fuller cost comparison framework, see our guide on measuring the ROI of AI video . Limitations Worth Stating The authors are explicit about the boundaries of this work, and the findings are more useful when those boundaries are respected. It was a descriptive study, not a controlled comparison. It did not test whether AI videos outperform human-recorded videos or written documentation. The 86% quiz average shows learning happened, not that it happened better. The students were enrolled in upper-level CS courses. Even though most had little Markdown experience, they had substantial background in programming and technical notation, which likely made the material easier to absorb. Results may differ for introductory learners. The content was simple and short. Three-minute videos on basic syntax are close to the ideal case for this format, and the students themselves flagged complex material as a poor fit. Nothing here says AI video handles advanced topics well. The qualitative themes come from one coding process and are open to other interpretations, which the authors acknowledge and address by publishing their codebook process and representative quotes. Disclosure Knowlify provided the research team with early access to the platform and complimentary video credits for this study. As stated in the paper's acknowledgements, Knowlify had no role in the study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, or the decision to publish. We are writing about this research because it is independent, and we think the parts that are unflattering to AI video are as interesting as the parts that are not. Key Takeaways 170 computing students at two US universities watched three AI-generated instructional videos built with Knowlify and rated them 4.52 out of 5 for production quality, 4.43 for accuracy, and 4.39 for helpfulness. Half the students could not clearly tell the videos were AI-generated, the highest-variance item in the survey. Students averaged 86% on a post-viewing knowledge test despite most having little or no prior familiarity with the topic. Support drops sharply at substitution: 68% would not prefer AI video over instructor-recorded video and 62% would not trust it equally. Students endorsed AI video for simple topics (27%), visual topics (15%), summaries (12%), and supplemental material (12%). Accuracy is the dominant concern at 58%, named more than four times as often as the next issue. Removing AI avatars appears to be a significant reason the videos were received well, since prior research found synthetic presenters distracting and uncanny. Each three-minute video took at most 25 minutes of combined design, generation, and human verification time. FAQ Do students like AI-generated instructional videos? Yes, when the videos supplement rather than replace instruction. In a 2026 study of 170 computing students, 92% agreed the AI-generated videos were professionally produced, 92% said the videos helped them understand the material, and 88% said the content was accurate. However, only 10% said they would prefer AI video over videos recorded by their own instructor, so approval is conditional on the videos being an addition rather than a substitution. Can students tell if a video is AI-generated? Often not. In the 2026 study, only 50% of upper-level computer science students agreed they could clearly tell the videos were AI-generated, while 35% disagreed and 15% were neutral. This was the only item in the survey without consensus. The videos used animated visual walkthroughs rather than AI avatars, which the researchers suggest is a key reason detection was so difficult, since synthetic faces and voices are the usual giveaway. Do students learn as well from AI-generated videos? Students in this study learned the material well, averaging 4.3 out of 5 (roughly 86%) on a knowledge test after watching, despite most reporting little or no prior familiarity with the topic. Platform logs confirmed they watched 76% to 81% of each video on average. Important caveat: the study was descriptive rather than comparative, so it measured short-term knowledge acquisition and did not test AI video against human-recorded video or written documentation. What topics work best for AI-generated educational videos? Students identified four categories. Simple or foundational topics such as vocabulary and basic syntax were named by 27% of students. Topics that benefit from visualization, such as data structures and step-by-step processes, were named by 15%. Topic summaries and exam review were named by 12%, and supplemental explanations that reinforce a concept a second way were also named by 12%. Students specifically flagged complex, subjective, and interactive topics as poor fits. What are students most concerned about with AI videos in education? Accuracy, by a wide margin. 58% of students raised concerns about inaccurate or hallucinated information, more than four times the rate of the next concern. After that came lack of depth (13%), lack of engagement (13%), reduced interaction with instructors (10%), and the sense that AI video undermines the value of tuition (10%). Only 6% of students reported no concerns at all. Should AI videos replace lectures? The students in this study said no, clearly. 68% disagreed that they would prefer AI videos over instructor-recorded videos, 62% disagreed that they would trust AI video equally, and 16% specifically named replacing instructor-led lectures as an inappropriate use. The researchers conclude that AI videos can play a meaningful role in education without displacing the instructor presence that students value. How long does it take to make an AI instructional video? In this study, each three-minute video took at most 25 minutes end to end. That breaks down as 8 to 11 minutes of planning, reviewing, and configuring, 3 minutes 48 seconds of average system generation time, and about 10 minutes of human verification. The researchers generated the videos by uploading GitHub's official Markdown documentation as a PDF to Knowlify and using a single prompt. Why did the researchers avoid AI avatars in the videos? To remove social presence as a confounding variable. Prior research had found students perceived AI-generated appearances and voices as distracting and uncanny, even when the script was identical to a human-produced version, which made it impossible to separate reactions to AI instruction from reactions to synthetic humans. By using animated visual walkthroughs with no talking heads, this study isolated the question of whether AI-generated instruction works. The high production-quality ratings suggest the choice mattered. References Knowlify learning science principles Student Perceptions and Preferences Regarding AI-Generated Instructional Videos in Computing Education turning technical documentation into video training video libraries new-hire onboarding programs Knowlify app measuring the ROI of AI video

title: Saga Communications, Inc. Reports 2nd Quarter 2026 Results
summary: GROSSE POINTE FARMS, Mich., Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Saga Communications, Inc. (Nasdaq - SGA) (the “Company” or “Saga”) today reported that net revenue decreased 6.5% to $26.4 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 compared to $28.2 million for the same period last year.
body_text: Release Details Saga Communications, Inc. Reports 2nd Quarter 2026 Results Aug 13, 2026 PDF Version GROSSE POINTE FARMS, Mich., Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Saga Communications, Inc. (Nasdaq - SGA) (the “Company” or “Saga”) today reported that net revenue decreased 6.5% to $26.4 million for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 compared to $28.2 million for the same period last year. Station operating expense increased 5.4% for the quarter to $23.4 million compared to the same period last year, or 3.9% excluding the non-cash rent expense disclosed below. For the quarter, we had operating income of $623 thousand compared to $1.4 million for the same quarter last year and station operating income (a non-GAAP financial measure) decreased 50.6% to $3.0 million. Capital expenditures totaled $1.3 million for the quarter which was comparable to the same period last year. We had net income of $960 thousand for the quarter compared to $1.1 million for the second quarter last year. Diluted earnings per share were $0.15 in the second quarter of 2026. Net revenue decreased 6.0% to $49.3 million for the six-month period ended June 30, 2026 compared to $52.4 million for the same period last year. Station operating expense increased 2.8% for the six-month period to $45.4 million compared to the same period last year, or 1.9% excluding the non-cash rent expense disclosed below. For the six-month period, we had an operating loss of $2.6 million compared to $889 thousand for the same period last year and station operating income (a non-GAAP financial measure) decreased 53.7% to $3.8 million. Capital expenditures for the six-months were $2.0 million which was comparable to the same period last year. We had a net loss of $1.4 million for the six-month period compared to $447 thousand for the same period last year. Diluted loss per share was $0.23 in the six-month period ending June 30, 2026. As previously reported, the Company sold 24 telecommunications towers, related real property and other assets located at 22 sites on October 17, 2025 and as amended in the quarter ended June 30, 2026 for a total cash purchase price of approximately $10.7 million, increasing our liquidity while retaining long term access to those assets with no cash expense. As part of this transaction, we are recording non-cash rent expense as a portion of station operating expense and non-cash interest income on our income statement. The structure of this transaction allows us to account for a portion of the taxable gain as an installment sale for tax purposes over the term of the lease agreements. We have included in the above results the impact that the non-cash rent expense has on our station operating expense. Based on the amendments the Company entered into we expect to report approximately $154 thousand per quarter of non-cash rent expense as a part of station operating expense for the term of the lease agreements and $127 thousand per quarter of non-cash interest income in 2026. The non-cash interest income will change annually reducing to a nominal value at the end of the full term of the lease agreements. For the quarter ended June 30, 2026 the Company recorded $352 thousand in non-cash rent expense which included $154 thousand for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, as well as $99 thousand for the quarter ended March 31, 2026 and $99 thousand for the quarter ended December 31, 2025 to recognize the impact of the amendments on previous quarters. The Company also recorded $381 thousand in non-cash interest income for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 which included $127 thousand for each of the quarters ended June 30, 2026, March 31, 2026 and December 31, 2025. The non-cash expense and non-cash income resulting from prior periods were a result of the accounting for the amendments to the Purchase Agreement and related documents. For the six-month period ended June 30, 2026 the Company recorded $407 thousand in non-cash rent expense and $381 thousand in non-cash interest income. This transaction will be more fully disclosed in our second quarter Form10-Q. The Company paid a quarterly dividend of $0.25 per share on June 12, 2026. The aggregate amount of the quarterly dividend was approximately $1.6 million. To date Saga has paid over $145 million in dividends to shareholders since the first special dividend was paid in 2012. The Company intends to pay regular quarterly cash dividends in the future. The Company’s balance sheet reflected $27.8 million in cash and short-term investments as of June 30, 2026. title: Steady CPI Report Calms Inflation Fears
summary: Cboe Global Markets, a leading provider of market infrastructure and tradable products, delivers cutting-edge trading, clearing and investment solutions to market participants around the world.
body_text: Article published at 8:55 a.m. CT, updated at 9:03 a.m. CT JJ Kinahan is Senior Vice President, Head of Retail Expansion and Alternative Investment Products at Cboe Global Markets, Inc. (Cboe). Key Takeaways: CPI numbers fall in line with projections Major indices reverse course to the upside Strong earnings power tech stocks The markets swung into positive territory in early trading and stayed there after the Consumer Price Index (CPI) soothed some inflation fears. The CPI report’s numbers exactly matched Wall Street’s expectations of inflation, easing slightly to 3.4%, with core inflation, which excludes volatile gas and energy costs, improving to 2.4%. Though core inflation is still above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target, the slippage from last month’s 2.5% reading gives the Central Bank some wiggle room. Inflation is the bigger worry for the Fed’s decision on the direction of interest rates, but last week’s weak job numbers are a factor as well. Still, with all the outside noise in play, we can view the economy in a positive light until some things are settled with the Iran situation. The CME FedWatch tool lightened up its look at an interest rate hike since yesterday, registering a 62% likelihood rates will stay steady at 3.5% to 3.75%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average is moving 0.05% to the upside, with the S&P 500 Index is rising 0.22% and the Nasdaq Composite advancing by 0.50%, holding on to pre-market gains, reversing the downtrend earlier this week. Investors appeared to be waiting for the CPI report before jumping in or out of aggressive trading. A handful of technology stocks are also fueling the market upside. Super Micro Computer assuaged Wall Street late Monday when it turned in profits that were nearly 90% higher than the year-ago period despite sales that fell short of expectations. The server company blamed delays in power, cooling and networking for the sales slip, but expects to make up the shortage in future quarters. Cash flow from operating activities was $747 million compared with a cash burn of $6.6 billion in the prior quarter. Net debt fell, too, to $1.2 billion compared with $7.5 billion in the third quarter, with cash and cash equivalents totaling $7.5 billion, the company said. Shares trekked 9.3% upward, right around its implied move. CoreWeave shares are in rally mode after the artificial intelligence (AI) firm turned in revenues that doubled year-over-year, beating Wall Street’s expectations and offering a look into how AI could be paying off. Losses were narrower than projected. Capital expenditures hit $9.4 billion, also exceeding the Street’s outlook and ballooning debt to $35 billion. CoreWeave upped its full-year revenue guidance, citing a $104 billion backlog, a sign of ongoing expansion. Shares continued their post-market expansion, trading 20% higher. Lumentum Holdings are tracking higher by nearly 10% after it reported that revenue more than doubled in its fiscal fourth quarter and profits cleared Wall Street’s expectations. However, the optical and photonic products maker reported a GAAP loss of $7.2 billion tied to converting certain debt into stock. Looking ahead, Lumentum’s forecast surpasses Wall Street’s estimates. Other tech stocks moving higher include Sandisk, up 6.2%, Micron at 4.3%, Intel rising by 2.9% and Nvidia stepping up by 1.3%. Investors are eating up Cava Group shares after the restaurant chain said same-store sales, a critical metric, was up 9% for the second straight quarter. That helped boost second-quarter profits and earnings above projections. The Mediterranean fast-casual chain said the backlash it experienced from the cyclospora outbreak – even though it does not serve iceberg lettuce – was rebounding. Shares were rebounding too, up 17% after falling some 32% since the food safety concerns first surfaced in early May. Despite the upbeat results, Cava maintained its forecast guidance, citing “macro and geopolitical uncertainty.” H&R Block shares are on the upswing by 13.5% after the tax preparation company raised its fiscal-year 2028 earnings and revenue outlook and upped its dividend 10%. Its fiscal fourth-quarter ended with sales lower on a year-over-year basis, but per-share earnings were higher, reflecting a mix of its client base, the company said. Keep an eye out for Cisco Systems fiscal fourth-quarter earnings report after the market closes. Investors are more likely to be interested in what the cloud networking giant has to say than what numbers it unveils. The options market is signaling an 8% implied move in either direction, meaning a high of $130.06 and a low of $110.80. Cisco shares are climbing toward 2% in early trading, up 58.4% year-to-date. Happy trading! 2026 Cboe Exchange, Inc. All rights reserved. The information provided is for general education and information purposes only. No statement provided should be construed as a recommendation to buy or sell a security, future, financial instrument, investment fund, or other investment product (collectively, a “financial product”), or to provide investment advice.
