title: The Founding of YouTube A Short History
summary: YouTube is one of the most influential platforms in modern media, but its origin story is surprisingly simple: a small team wanted an easier way to share video online. In the early 2000s, uploading and sending video files was slow, formats were inconsistent, and most websites weren’t built for smooth playback. YouTube’s founders focused on removing
body_text: YouTube is one of the most influential platforms in modern media, but its origin story is surprisingly simple: a small team wanted an easier way to share video online. In the early 2000s, uploading and sending video files was slow, formats were inconsistent, and most websites weren’t built for smooth playback. YouTube’s founders focused on removing those barriers—making video sharing as easy as sending a link. Who Founded YouTube? YouTube was founded by three former PayPal employees: Chad Hurley , Steve Chen , and Jawed Karim . They combined product thinking, engineering skills, and a clear user goal: create a website where anyone could upload a video and watch it instantly in a browser. Chad Hurley — product/design focus and early CEO role Steve Chen — engineering and infrastructure Jawed Karim — engineering and early concept support The Problem YouTube Solved At the time, sharing video often meant emailing huge files or dealing with complicated players and downloads. YouTube made video: Uploadable by non-experts (simple interface) Streamable in the browser (no special setup) Sharable through links and embedding on other sites Early Growth and the First Video YouTube launched publicly in 2005. One of the most famous early moments was the first uploaded video, “Me at the zoo,” featuring co-founder Jawed Karim. The clip was short and casual—exactly the kind of everyday content that proved the platform’s big idea: ordinary people could publish video without needing a studio. Key Milestones Timeline Year/Date Milestone Why It Mattered 2005 YouTube is founded and launches Introduced easy browser-based video sharing 2005 “Me at the zoo” is uploaded Became a symbol of user-generated video culture 2006 Google acquires YouTube Provided resources to scale hosting and global reach Why Google Bought YouTube By 2006, YouTube’s traffic was exploding. Video hosting is expensive—bandwidth and storage costs rise fast when millions of people watch content daily. Google’s acquisition gave YouTube the infrastructure and advertising ecosystem to grow into a sustainable business. What YouTube’s Founding Changed YouTube didn’t just create a popular website; it reshaped how people learn, entertain themselves, and build careers online. Its founding helped accelerate: Creator-driven media and influencer culture How-to education and free tutorials at massive scale Music discovery, commentary, and global community trends From a small startup idea to a global video powerhouse, YouTube’s founding is a classic example of a simple product solving a real problem—and changing the internet in the process.

title: LPL Financial Opens Focus 2026 Conference
summary: LPL Financial kicks off Focus 2026, uniting thousands of advisors for three days of growth, innovation, and the future of wealth management. Learn more.
body_text: LPL Financial Opens Focus 2026, Bringing Together Thousands of Advisors to Explore the Future of Wealth Management Firm showcases investments in AI, cybersecurity and wealth management solutions designed to help financial professionals thrive in a rapidly evolving industry Last Edited by: LPL Financial Last Updated: August 10, 2026 SAN DIEGO – August 10, 2026 – LPL Financial LLC kicked off Focus 2026 yesterday, the firm’s premier annual conference, bringing together thousands of financial advisors, institutional leaders and industry professionals for three days focused on growth, innovation and the future of the wealth management industry. The conference theme, Unlocking Boundless Human Potential , explores how innovation across technology, wealth management and client experiences can help financial professionals strengthen relationships, grow their businesses and deliver more value. In his keynote address, LPL Financial Chief Executive Officer Rich Steinmeier described how transformative technologies have historically replaced tasks, not professions. Drawing parallels to innovations that reshaped industries throughout history, Steinmeier said AI represents the next evolution of advice, helping advisors unlock administrative capacity so they can focus more on the uniquely human elements of their profession, including judgment, client relationships, empathy and personalized guidance. Speaking to a crowd of more than 6,000 advisors, Steinmeier said, “Will AI replace the advisor? Quite simply, no. Those who embrace AI will become more valuable. The future of advice is more human. Our investments in technology and AI are designed to help advisors spend less time on routine tasks and more time helping clients navigate life's most important financial decisions." Chief Client Officer Matt Enyedi highlighted investments designed to help advisors operate more efficiently and deliver a better client experience, including enhanced cybersecurity protections, expanded mobile access, improved communication tools, a more client-centric operating system for advisors and streamlined account management capabilities. "When advisors have the right experience, everything changes,” said Enyedi. “Our role is to remove friction and make it easier for our clients to run their businesses, serve their clients and pursue growth on their own terms. Every innovation we deliver is designed to help advisors spend less time navigating systems and more time creating meaningful outcomes." The general session concluded with a presentation from Chief Technology and Information Officer Greg Gates , who highlighted LPL's nearly $2 billion investment over the past three years to modernize its technology infrastructure, strengthen cybersecurity and establish the foundation for scaling AI across the advisor experience. Central to that strategy is LPL Latitude , the firm's unified technology experience that brings together data, workflows, cybersecurity and intelligence to create a more seamless advisor experience and power future innovation. Gates described Latitude as more than a traditional technology system, positioning it as a fundamental evolution in how LPL delivers technology to advisors. Rather than deploying AI as a standalone tool, LPL is embedding intelligence directly into advisor workflows to deliver more personalized, relevant and actionable support. Gates also demonstrated Cyan , LPL's AI agent and a core asset of Latitude, which is designed to enhance advisor efficiency by providing contextual guidance, surfacing timely insights and streamlining everyday tasks within ClientWorks, LPL’s advisor operating system. Future capabilities are expected to support financial planning workflows, generate personalized client meeting materials for review and deliver practice management insights designed to help advisors identify growth opportunities. Looking ahead, Gates shared LPL's vision for a more proactive, agentic AI experience in which Cyan not only informs and guides, but also helps advisors take action, by initiating workflows, preparing draft communications and identifying opportunities directly within their daily work. By doing so, Cyan will give advisors more time to focus on what matters most: delivering personalized advice, deepening client relationships and growing their businesses. “The best technology isn't technology that shows off what we can build,” said Gates. “It's technology that understands people and helps make their lives better. And that idea — that the most powerful technology is human centered — has shaped how we innovate at LPL.” As Focus 2026 continues, attendees will hear from LPL leaders on the transformative opportunities shaping the future of advice, including AI, market dynamics, service innovation and partnership, all aligned to the firm's vision of helping advisors unlock boundless human potential. The firm provides a wide range of advisor affiliation models, investment solutions, fintech tools and practice management services, ensuring that advisors and institutions have the flexibility to choose the business model, services, and technology resources they need to run thriving businesses. title: How to Make Healthy Food Choices Easier for Families
summary: Discover practical ways families can make healthier food choices, from affordable shopping and better food labelling to healthier school meals and industry action. body_text: Discover practical ways families can make healthier food choices, from affordable shopping and better food labelling to healthier school meals and industry action. How Can Families Make Healthier Food Choices? Helping children and families eat a healthier diet is not simply about telling people what they should and should not eat. For many households, the reality is much more complicated. Food prices, busy schedules, confusing labels, advertising and the availability of convenient products can all influence what ends up on the family table. Recent discussions involving nutrition experts, health organisations, food companies and retailers have highlighted an important point: healthier eating needs to become easier, more affordable and more practical for families. The issue is particularly significant in the UK, where concerns about childhood obesity and diet-related health conditions continue to grow. The World Obesity Atlas 2026, cited in a recent Guardian feature, reported that around 3.8 million children in the UK have a high BMI. Rather than placing responsibility entirely on parents, experts argue that supermarkets, manufacturers, policymakers and wider society all have a role to play. Why Healthy Eating Can Be Difficult for Families Most parents want to provide nutritious meals for their children. However, good intentions do not always translate into easy decisions at the supermarket. Parents often have to balance nutrition with price, convenience and what their children will actually eat. Food packaging can also make choosing between products difficult, particularly when claims such as "natural", "high in fibre" or "no added sugar" appear prominently on the front of a packet. Paediatric dietitian Lucy Upton has highlighted how confusing food information can leave parents feeling uncertain about whether they are making the right choices. Affordability is another major concern. Research highlighted by the Food Foundation suggests that healthier diets can be significantly more expensive for families on lower incomes. This means that simply advising households to buy healthier foods may not address the underlying problem. A successful approach needs to consider household budgets as well as nutritional guidelines. Making Healthy Food More Affordable One of the most effective ways to encourage healthier eating may be to make nutritious food easier to afford. Fresh fruit and vegetables, wholegrains, pulses and other nutritious ingredients should be accessible to families across different income levels. Promotions and pricing strategies can influence purchasing decisions, especially when households are trying to manage a weekly food budget. Retailers can contribute by increasing the availability of affordable healthier options and making these products easier to identify. Tesco, for example, has reported initiatives designed to increase the proportion of its food sales classified as healthy. The supermarket has also highlighted promotions involving fruit, vegetables and everyday essentials. However, affordability should not depend entirely on individual supermarket initiatives. Government policy and wider food-system changes may be necessary if healthier diets are to become genuinely accessible to everyone. Helping Children Develop Healthy Eating Habits Healthy eating for children is not about creating a perfect diet. Children need a balanced range of foods, and their preferences can change over time. Families can encourage healthier habits by regularly offering fruit and vegetables, choosing wholegrain foods where appropriate, including sources of protein and keeping sugary foods and drinks as occasional choices. Presentation can also make a difference. Children are often attracted to food because of its appearance, branding and familiarity. Making nutritious foods appealing and enjoyable can therefore be an important part of encouraging better choices. Experts have suggested that healthier foods need to compete with the excitement created by heavily marketed packaged products. This does not mean turning every meal into a complicated recipe. Simple ideas such as colourful fruit, vegetable snacks, homemade sandwiches or easy family meals can make healthy food feel normal rather than restrictive. Understanding Ultra-Processed Foods Ultra-processed foods, commonly referred to as UPFs, have become a major part of discussions about modern diets. Some experts are concerned about the high proportion of ultra-processed foods consumed by children and teenagers in the UK. The challenge, however, is that not every packaged food should automatically be treated as unhealthy. Nutrition is more complicated than simply dividing food into "good" and "bad" categories. Families can instead focus on overall dietary patterns and aim to include a wide variety of minimally processed foods. Reading nutrition information, comparing products and paying attention to ingredients can help, but food labelling needs to be clear enough for busy shoppers to understand quickly. What Can Supermarkets and Food Manufacturers Do? Food companies have considerable influence over what consumers see, buy and eat. Reformulating products to reduce excessive sugar, salt or saturated fat can therefore make a difference without requiring families to completely change their routines. Tesco has reported efforts to increase fibre, reduce sugar in selected products and modify children's yoghurt products. Such initiatives demonstrate how changes made at the manufacturing and retail level can potentially affect large numbers of consumers. Food manufacturers can also help by improving product information and making healthier products more visible. Clearer standards could provide companies with greater certainty about what constitutes a healthier product. Consistent government guidelines could also make it easier for consumers to compare foods. The Role of Government Policy Experts involved in the recent discussion argued that education alone may not be enough to create large-scale improvements in population health. People can be given nutritional advice, but their choices are still influenced by the environment around them. If healthier foods are expensive, difficult to find or heavily out-marketed, information alone may have limited impact. Government policy could therefore focus on measures that encourage healthier products, improve food standards and reduce the marketing of less healthy foods to children. Mandatory reporting and measurable targets have also been suggested as ways to encourage businesses to make meaningful changes. The goal should not be to make healthy eating complicated. Instead, the food environment should make healthier decisions easier by default. Small Changes Can Add Up Improving family nutrition does not require every household to completely transform its diet overnight. Small, sustainable changes can be easier to maintain. Families might start by adding an extra portion of vegetables to dinner, replacing some sugary drinks with water or choosing wholegrain alternatives more often. Planning a few meals in advance can also reduce reliance on takeaway food during busy evenings. Cooking larger portions and using leftovers for another meal may help families save both time and money. The most important point is consistency rather than perfection. A Shared Responsibility for Healthier Families The challenge of improving children's diets cannot rest entirely on parents. Families make choices within an environment shaped by food prices, product availability, advertising, packaging and public policy. Supermarkets can make healthier options more affordable and visible. Manufacturers can reformulate products. Schools can support nutritious meals and food education. Governments can create clearer standards and policies. Parents can encourage balanced eating habits at home. When these efforts work together, healthier choices can become part of everyday life rather than another source of pressure for busy families. Creating a healthier food environment will take time, investment and cooperation. But the principle is straightforward: families should not have to be nutrition experts, spend excessive amounts of money or devote hours to cooking every day simply to provide their children with a balanced diet. Making healthier choices easier, clearer and more affordable could be one of the most practical ways to support the health of future generations. Sources The Guardian, published 17 July 2026. World Obesity Atlas 2026, World Obesity Federation. The Food Foundation, The Broken Plate 2026 . National Institute for Health and Care Research, research on ultra-processed food consumption among UK adolescents. British Heart Foundation, information on obesity and cardiovascular disease. Nesta, research on modest reductions in calorie intake and obesity prevention. Disclaimer This article is for general informational and educational purposes only. It is based on publicly available information and the source material provided for this article. It is not medical, nutritional or dietary advice and should not replace guidance from a qualified healthcare professional or registered dietitian. Individual nutritional needs vary, particularly for children, and parents or carers should seek professional advice when they have concerns about a child's growth, diet or health.

title: A Bigger Bench: How Recidiviz is Partnering with Nonprofits to Scale Reentry Support
summary: Opportunities is now live across every state correctional facility in Arizona, through our partnership with Edovo—a digital learning platform that gives incarcerated people access to free educational, vocational, and personal development content. To date, over 29,000 individuals in Arizona have accessed the app. That statewide reach is what makes the partnerships with Inside Out Network (ION) and CEO possible, helping us connect people to new resources at exactly the right moment before release.
body_text: The window before release is one of the most important moments in a person's reentry journey. People preparing to come home are often motivated, ready to plan, and open to building skills. But access to the right resources at the right time remains a persistent gap. We've heard this directly from incarcerated individuals: ‍ ‍ "I would like to suggest that you add a bullet point outline of what us residents need to have prepared in order to meet [sentence] dates. Such as home plan, employment, transportation." — Incarcerated individual in Arizona "Would like to be able to learn about specific job skills in the field i want to work in and be able to communicate with someone in that field thats willing to help." — Incarcerated individual in Arkansas “I think about my family and getting home as soon as possible. I want to show my charge does not define me im just a human who made a mistake and am ready for change." — Incarcerated individual in North Dakota We've been working with other nonprofits to explore how reentry tools and resources from trusted organizations can reach people when it matters most, in the period before release, through Recidiviz's Opportunities app . Opportunities is a tablet app that improves transparency by putting key sentence dates and reentry pathways on the tablets incarcerated people already use inside correctional facilities. It’s now live in eight states, where more than 80,000 people are using the app to get essential information about their timeline and progress so they can take ownership of their reentry journey. Incarcerated individuals have already shared that the app has helped to increase understanding around key dates and what programs exist, as well as what steps they can take to prepare for reentry. "The information provided was straightforward and precise, offering clarity and peace of mind to everyone. It has enhanced our understanding of various sentence dates." —Incarcerated individual in Arizona “It helps better track my parole date and me when I should take the next steps for being able to go home.” —Incarcerated individual in North Dakota “I favorited specific programs I might be interested in and gained more intel on others I hadn't know existed.” —Incarcerated individual in Arkansas ‍ Providing key sentence information is just the beginning for the Opportunities app. Earlier this year, we announced our first reentry resource network partners —the Center for Employment Opportunities (CEO), FreeWorld, mRelief, and SkillUp Coalition—in our case planning tool for supervision staff. We're building on that foundation by bringing these partnerships into the Opportunities app so that people can access them directly. And that’s just the start; we’re adding two new integrations in Arizona. Expanding Our Arizona Partnerships Opportunities is now live across every state correctional facility in Arizona, through our partnership with Edovo —a digital learning platform that gives incarcerated people access to free educational, vocational, and personal development content. To date, over 29,000 individuals in Arizona have accessed the app. That statewide reach is what makes the partnerships with Inside Out Network (ION) and CEO possible, helping us connect people to new resources at exactly the right moment before release. ‍ "Every person who comes home prepared—with a job prospect, a place to live, a support network—is less likely to return to our system. That's good for them, good for their families, and good for Arizona communities. Partnerships in Opportunities like these with CEO and Inside Out Network will give people in our facilities that head start, and we're proud to be part of making that possible." —Dr. Ryan Thornell, Director, Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation and Reentry New Partnership: Inside Out Network The Inside Out Network (ION) , an Arizona-based nonprofit, has built something critical: an online platform that empowers incarcerated people and service providers to find and connect with each other. Through ION, people leaving prison can search and message directly with second-chance employers, housing providers, vocational training programs, health care providers, and more. In 2025 alone, ION connected over 4,000 people with several hundred service providers, facilitating over 56,000 searches and more than 54,000 messages between the two. What makes ION distinctive is that it's built for active connection. It’s a live network where both sides of a reentry interaction can see, be seen, be proactive, and make relevant, timely, and meaningful connections. Our partnership with ION starts with a simple, high-value step: when someone in the Opportunities app is eleven months from their release date, we'll surface a notification recommending they create an ION account. Getting connected to a provider network, and being able to message with them, before release—not after—can meaningfully change how the first weeks at home go. Over time, we plan to integrate ION more directly into Opportunities. Deepening Our Partnership with CEO in Arizona We started partnering with the Center for Employment Opportunities (CEO) earlier this year, when they joined our provider network. CEO is the largest reentry employment provider in the United States, operating in 30 cities across 12 states, exclusively serving people who have recently been released from incarceration. Now we're extending that partnership through the Opportunities app to reach people before release. In the pivotal months leading up to that moment—when people are starting to think seriously about employment and how to land a job—we'll connect them to two of CEO's resources available through the Edovo platform, starting in Arizona: Job-search preparation. Through Edovo, CEO offers educational content designed to help people navigate the job market after incarceration, including the LinkedIn Learning course, "Job Seeking with a Criminal Record," developed in partnership with CEO specifically for justice-involved learners. These resources help people understand how to highlight their skills, address employment gaps, and approach employers with confidence. CEO's AI Voice Coach. CEO has developed a secure, phone-based AI coaching tool that incarcerated individuals can use 24/7 through existing monitored phone lines. People can practice job interviews, workplace communication, and conflict resolution in a low-stakes, judgment-free environment and receive real-time feedback. CEO built this tool with input from people directly impacted by the justice system, incorporating clear guardrails, privacy protections, and staged piloting. In early pilots across 500+ participants, CEO's AI Voice Coach improved people’s interview skills and reduced their pre-interview anxiety. Importantly, staff shared positive feedback that the AI Voice Coach enhances, not replaces, their own coaching. What This Looks Like for People Using Opportunities The sooner reentry planning begins, the better a person’s chances of success. Consider someone in Arizona, eleven months from release. They open the Opportunities app on Edovo and see a prompt to create an ION account and start building connections with employers, support groups, and housing providers. A few months later, they're practicing interviews with CEO's AI Voice Coach, exploring career pathways through SkillUp, learning how to get their Social Security card through FreeWorld, and finding out if they qualify for SNAP through mRelief and enrolling in benefits. By the time they walk out the door, they've taken multiple concrete steps to prepare for reentry. That's what these partnerships and the tools in Opportunities are designed to make possible: preparation that's actionable, not just informational. This network is still growing. We're working to expand coverage across more geographies and add partners to address more of the barriers to successful reentry. By collaborating with mission-aligned nonprofits, we’re expanding our collective reach and maximizing the impact for every person coming home. About Our Partners Center for Employment Opportunities The Center for Employment Opportunities (CEO) provides immediate, effective, and comprehensive employment services exclusively to people recently released from incarceration. CEO currently operates in 30 cities in 12 states and is dedicated to ensuring that justice-impacted people have opportunities and careers to achieve socioeconomic mobility. Learn more → Edovo The largest digital learning platform for incarcerated people, Edovo provides free educational, vocational, and personal development content to more than 1.1 million learners. By transforming correctional environments through technology, Edovo helps individuals build skills and prepare for a successful return to their communities. Opportunities is available through Edovo in Arizona and in six other states. Learn more → Inside Out Network The Inside Out Network (ION) is an Arizona-based nonprofit that connects people leaving incarceration with reentry service providers, second-chance employers, housing, and community support through a live online platform. ION operates across Arizona, Illinois, Oregon, and Mississippi, and has connected more than 12,000 returning citizens with over 600 service providers. Learn more →

title: Cherry Hill Mortgage Investment Corporation Announces Second Quarter 2026 Results
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about Cherry Hill Mortgage Investment Corporation's business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: Cherry Hill Mortgage Investment Corporation Announces Second Quarter 2026 Results Aug 10, 2026 PDF Version TINTON FALLS, N.J.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 10, 2026-- Cherry Hill Mortgage Investment Corporation (NYSE: CHMI) (“Cherry Hill” or the “Company”) today reported results for the second quarter 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Highlights and Subsequent Events GAAP net income applicable to common stockholders of $1.3 million, or $0.04 per share. Earnings available for distribution (“EAD”) attributable to common stockholders of $5.5 million, or $0.15 per diluted share. Common book value per share of $3.16 at June 30, 2026. Declared regular common dividend of $0.10 per share; annualized common dividend yield was 16.6% based on the closing sale price of the Company’s common stock as reported by the NYSE on August 7, 2026. Aggregate portfolio leverage stood at 5.02x at June 30, 2026. As of June 30, 2026, the Company had unrestricted cash of $52.1 million. On August 10, 2026, the Company announced the entry into a definitive merger agreement with TPG Mortgage Investment Trust, Inc. (NYSE: MITT) (“MITT”) with an implied transaction value of $117.5 million, representing a 29% premium to closing price on August 7, 2026, and a 32% premium to 30-Day Volume Weighted Average Price (“VWAP”). Due to the pending transaction, the Company will not be hosting its webcast and conference call. Operating Results Cherry Hill reported GAAP net income applicable to common stockholders for the second quarter of 2026 of $1.3 million, or $0.04 per basic and diluted weighted average common share outstanding. Reported GAAP net income was determined based primarily on the following: $4.7 million of net interest income, $7.4 million of net servicing income, $1.0 million of net realized loss on RMBS, a net realized gain of $12.1 million on derivatives, a net unrealized loss of $0.9 million on RMBS measured at fair value through earnings, a net unrealized loss of $9.3 million on derivatives, a net unrealized loss of $2.4 million on investments in Servicing Related Assets, credit loss and impairment on other assets of $2.8 million, and general and administrative expenses and compensation and benefits in the aggregate amount of $4.0 million. Portfolio Highlights for the Quarter Ended June 30, 2026 The Company realized net servicing fee income of $7.4 million, net interest income of $4.7 million and other loss of $4.2 million, primarily related to a realized loss on RMBS, an unrealized loss on RMBS, an unrealized loss on derivatives, an unrealized loss on investments in Servicing Related Assets, and a credit loss and impairment on other assets, partially offset by a realized gain on derivatives. The unpaid principal balance for the MSR portfolio stood at $15.2 billion as of June 30, 2026 and the carrying value of the MSR portfolio ended the quarter at $211.1 million. Net interest spread for the RMBS portfolio stood at 3.45% and the debt-to-equity ratio on the aggregate portfolio ended the quarter at 5.02x. The RMBS portfolio had a book value and carrying value of approximately $1.1 billion at quarter-end June 30, 2026. The portfolio had a weighted average coupon of 5.08% and weighted average maturity of 27 years. In order to mitigate duration risk and interest rate risk associated with the Company’s RMBS and MSRs, Cherry Hill used interest rate swaps, TBAs, Treasury futures and Eris SOFR swap futures. At quarter end June 30, 2026, the Company held interest rate swaps with a notional amount of $767.3 million, TBAs with a notional amount of ($266.9) million, Treasury futures with a notional amount of $28.4 million and Eris SOFR swap futures with a notional amount of ($82.0) million. As of June 30, 2026, Cherry Hill’s GAAP book value was $3.16 per diluted share, net of the second quarter dividend. Dividends On June 11, 2026, the Board of Directors declared a quarterly dividend of $0.10 per share of common stock for the second quarter of 2026. The dividend was paid in cash on July 31, 2026 to common stockholders of record as of the close of business on June 30, 2026. Additionally, the Board of Directors declared a dividend of $0.5125 per share on the Company’s 8.20% Series A Cumulative Redeemable Preferred Stock and a dividend of $0.6045 per share on the Company’s 8.250% Series B Fixed-to-Floating Rate Cumulative Redeemable Preferred Stock for the second quarter 2026. The dividends were paid in cash on July 15, 2026 to holders of the applicable Series of Preferred Stock of record as of the close of business on June 30, 2026. Merger On August 9, 2026, MITT, a publicly listed residential mortgage REIT managed by AG REIT Management, LLC, an affiliate of TPG Inc. (NASDAQ: TPG), a leading global alternative asset management firm with $327 billion in assets under management, and Cherry Hill Mortgage Investment Corporation entered into a definitive merger agreement, pursuant to which MITT will acquire CHMI. In connection with the transaction, holders of CHMI common stock will receive 0.3063 shares of MITT common stock and $0.93 in cash per share. Based on the closing price of MITT’s common stock on the New York Stock Exchange (the “NYSE”) on August 7, 2026, the transaction implies a value of $3.10 per share of CHMI common stock, representing a 29% premium to CHMI’s unaffected closing stock price on the NYSE on August 7, 2026. The companies expect the transaction to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions, including the approval of both MITT and CHMI stockholders. This strategic transaction was unanimously approved by the Board of Directors of MITT and Board of Directors of CHMI. Earnings Available for Distribution Earnings available for distribution (“EAD”) is a non-GAAP financial measure that we define as GAAP net income (loss), excluding realized gain (loss) on RMBS, unrealized gain (loss) on RMBS measured at fair value through earnings, realized and unrealized gain (loss) on derivatives, realized gain (loss) on acquired assets, realized and unrealized gain (loss) on investments in MSRs (net of any estimated MSR amortization), credit loss and impairment on other assets, transaction related expenses and any tax expense (benefit) on realized and unrealized gain (loss) on MSRs. MSR amortization refers to the portion of the change in fair value of the MSR that is primarily due to the realization of cashflows, runoff resulting from prepayments and an adjustment for any gain or loss on the capital used to purchase the MSR. EAD also includes interest rate swap periodic interest income (expense) and drop income on TBA dollar roll transactions, which are included in “Realized gain (loss) on derivatives, net” on the consolidated statements of income (loss). EAD is adjusted to exclude outstanding LTIP-OP Units in our Operating Partnership and dividends paid on our preferred stock. EAD is provided for purposes of potential comparability to other issuers that invest in residential mortgage-related assets. We believe providing investors with EAD, in addition to related GAAP financial measures, may provide investors some insight into our ongoing operational performance. However, the concept of EAD does have significant limitations, including the exclusion of realized and unrealized gains (losses), and given the apparent lack of a consistent methodology among issuers for defining EAD, it may not be comparable to similarly titled measures of other issuers, which define EAD differently from us and each other. As a result, EAD should not be considered a substitute for our GAAP net income (loss) or as a measure of our liquidity. While EAD is one indicia of the Company’s earnings capacity, it is not the only factor considered in setting a dividend and is not the same as REIT taxable income which is calculated in accordance with the rules of the IRS. title: 10 Project Management Templates for Agencies & Services 2026
summary: Find the right project management templates for your agency. Our curated list covers plans, roadmaps, and reports to help you standardize your team's workflow.
body_text: Stop reinventing the project plan for every new client. Your team just landed work, kickoff is next week, and now someone has to build the scope doc, timeline, status format, and handoff notes from scratch. That usually means wasted time, messy reporting, and a lot of documents that almost match each other but never quite do. The better move is to use project management templates that already reflect the way your agency or services team works, then tighten them into a small set that supports intake, delivery, billing, and reporting without extra noise. For mid-sized agencies and professional services firms, the test isn't whether a template looks clean. It's whether it helps the team start faster, keep ownership clear, and keep reporting consistent enough that leadership can trust it. The right set also helps reduce the gap between planning and the calendar, which matters when work happens across meetings, client calls, reviews, and billable time. If you want a broader agency workflow around prospecting and outreach, agency outreach with Extrovert is a useful adjacent read. 1. Asana Asana works well when you want a polished starting point without building your own structure from zero. Its template library covers campaign plans, project schedules, sprint planning, client onboarding, PMO work, and status reporting, so it fits teams that move between marketing, creative, and client delivery work. The biggest win is speed. You can duplicate a strong template, keep the same view structure, and get the team moving before kickoff drifts into admin. Asana's template library also helps when you need a repeatable setup across multiple teams. List, board, timeline, and calendar views carry into new projects, so the team doesn't have to rebuild the same layout every time. That matters for agencies because the same client can touch account, strategy, design, and delivery, and each group needs the same project with a different angle. Where it fits best Standardized client launches: Good when you need a clean client project shell with tasks, dates, and owners. Cross-functional delivery: Useful when one project has many contributors and you want the same structure every time. Template governance: Works better when one team owns the standards and other teams copy from approved versions. Asana's downside is also the thing that makes it flexible. If you don't govern the library, template sprawl creeps in fast. That creates a second problem, because teams stop trusting the templates and go back to ad hoc docs. The best practice is to keep a short approved set for common work, then lock down naming, fields, and required sections so everyone starts from the same base. Practical rule: use Asana when your pain is inconsistent setup, not when you need deep financial or utilization logic inside the template itself. 2. monday.com A mid-sized agency brings in a new client, and the first week usually exposes the same problem, intake lives in email, approvals sit in chat, and delivery starts before billing knows how the work is being tracked. monday.com helps clean up that handoff because the template gallery is built around projects, requests, approvals, customer work, timelines, and portfolio views. That makes it easier to standardize intake-to-delivery without forcing account teams or creative leads to work inside a heavy PM system. The monday.com template category also matters once the work needs to connect to reporting. Boards, calendar views, Gantt-style planning, and dashboards give managers a faster read on status than a stack of spreadsheets, and that matters when different client teams need the same structure but different owners and deadlines. If your team still starts in Excel, then spends time reconciling the live version later, importing that work into template boards can reduce cleanup and keep the source of truth in one place. What I'd use it for Client intake boards: Standardize request capture before work starts, then route the request to the right service team. Approval flows: Keep stakeholders out of long email threads and make sign-off visible in the same board. Portfolio rollups: Give managers a quick view across active accounts, which helps when billing and status reporting need to stay aligned. The trade-off is cost and complexity. Some useful views and automations sit behind higher tiers, and seat bundles can feel heavy for smaller teams. That said, if you run several client work streams and want the same visual system across intake, delivery, and reporting, monday.com usually gets adoption faster than tools that ask people to work from a stricter, text-first setup. 3. ClickUp An agency that delivers monthly reporting to five clients needs a template that carries the workflow, not just a task list. ClickUp is built for that kind of setup. It has 1,000+ templates , including agile, Scrum, consulting, compliance, roadmaps, client project plans, and deliverables. For agencies and services firms, that range matters because one team may need a simple launch plan while another needs a full delivery playbook with docs, tasks, dashboards, and automations in one place. ClickUp works well when the template has to standardize intake, delivery, and reporting together. You can save your own workflows as reusable templates, so a client onboarding setup or repeatable campaign process does not need to be rebuilt every quarter. That matters in agencies where handoffs move between sales, delivery, and reporting, and where billing depends on work being recorded the same way every time. Teams that want one operating model across recurring client work can use it to keep service lines aligned without forcing every project manager to invent their own structure. For mid-sized agencies, the practical value is consistency. If you standardize a small set of templates by service line, then tie them to status updates, time tracking, and billing codes, ClickUp can handle repeatable client work with less cleanup at the end of the month. It also gives operations teams a place to control naming, permissions, and required fields, which helps keep reporting clean when several accounts share the same delivery model. The trade-off is choice overload. A large library sounds helpful until nobody agrees on which template to use, so governance matters here more than in lighter tools. Put a standard set in place, limit templates by service line, and review them against how your team tracks time and reports client work. ClickUp becomes much more useful once the templates are managed as part of the workflow instead of treated as one-off starting points. 4. Smartsheet Smartsheet is the best fit when your team lives close to spreadsheets but needs stronger governance than a spreadsheet alone can provide. Its template gallery includes Template Sets for PMO and portfolio work, project tracking, risk logs, RAID, dashboards, and intake forms. That makes it a strong option for agencies that need structured reporting across multiple projects without forcing everyone into a completely new way of thinking. The value is the end-to-end pattern. You can move from intake to project creation, then roll up reporting in a format leadership can review without chasing the PM for a separate slide deck. The familiar sheet-based model also lowers friction for operations teams that already use Excel-style planning. For that reason, Smartsheet often works well when the main problem is not project thinking, but project consistency. The template should match the way your team already handles work, or people will rebuild it in a side file and the system breaks. The trade-off is admin weight. If your team doesn't already work in Smartsheet, setup can feel heavier than lighter task tools. It's also easy to overbuild the structure, which creates more upkeep than value. For agencies with portfolio reporting, intake controls, and standardized rollups, though, it's one of the more practical choices. You can also pair it with a simpler operating discipline, like the checklist approach in project management checklists , if your team needs to keep the execution side lean. 5. Wrike A client submits a new campaign request, the account lead approves the scope, and production needs to know who owns each step before work starts. Wrike fits that kind of handoff. Its template set covers IT, marketing, professional services, product delivery, and manufacturing, so agencies can standardize different service lines without rebuilding the workflow every time. The focus is less on polished presentation and more on repeatable routing, intake control, and visibility. The Wrike templates page is useful when workload views, proofing, and reporting have to live in the same workspace. Managers can see where work is blocked, who owns it, and which projects need attention before deadlines slip. That also makes capacity conversations more grounded, because workload views surface pressure points early instead of after the team is already overloaded. A mid-sized agency usually gets the most value from Wrike when it uses the templates to standardize the workload view, then ties that view to intake, approval, and reporting. That creates a shared operating picture for account teams, production, and leadership. It also makes billing and status reporting easier to reconcile, since the same template structure can carry the request details, ownership, and progress notes the finance or ops team needs later. Wrike can feel heavy for simple jobs, and that is the trade-off. If you only need a quick client tracker, it may be more than you need. If you need a template system that supports standardization across intake, capacity, and reporting, it earns its keep. 6. Airtable The account lead needs a clean intake form. The PM needs a workable board or timeline. The CFO wants a rollup that shows what is approved, what is underway, and what is waiting on billing. Airtable handles that kind of split view well because the same project data can sit behind different interfaces without forcing every team to work in the same layout. The Airtable template library includes project tracking, portfolio planning, resource allocation, and stakeholder templates, which makes it a smart fit for agencies that manage many client fields and need different views for different roles. Account teams, operations, and leadership can each see the same record set in a different shape, so the template becomes part of the operating model instead of just a place to store tasks. The main strength is the schema. You can map client, project, task, and approval data to match how the agency runs, then expose only the fields each person needs. Forms handle intake, automations cut down on repetitive updates, and interfaces keep stakeholders out of the full base while still giving them something usable. That matters when internal teams need detail, but clients or executives only need a summary that they can act on quickly. Airtable also helps standardization if you treat templates as a shared system, not a one-off setup. Define the same fields for scope, status, owner, due date, and billing trigger across service lines, then build views that support account management, production, and reporting. That makes handoffs easier to audit and gives operations a cleaner path to reconcile project updates with time tracking and invoice prep. The downside is discipline. Once a base grows, someone has to keep the model tidy, limit field sprawl, and decide which requests belong in the template and which do not. Airtable works best when a team owns governance and keeps the system from turning into a catch-all for every new idea. 7. Trello A six-person studio can get a client board live in Trello before lunch, which is why it stays useful for project management templates that need to work right away. The template gallery covers project management, process tracking, and content calendar boards, and that narrow focus suits mid-sized agencies that want a standard way to run repeatable work without forcing every team into a heavy system. For simple delivery, one board per client or one board per service line is often enough. The value is how fast a team can standardize it. Copy a board with one click, add Butler automations where the handoffs repeat, and bring in time tracking or reporting through Power-Ups only when the workflow needs that extra layer. That keeps setup light for account teams, and it also gives operations a practical path to tie task progress back to billing and reporting without rebuilding the whole process. A Trello template starts to strain when the work stops being linear. Dependencies become awkward to manage without add-ons, portfolio rollups are limited, and reporting usually needs another tool or a manual export. That is the trade-off. Trello is easy to adopt and easy to keep consistent, but teams that need deeper scheduling or stronger cross-project visibility usually have to pair it with something else. 8. Miro Miro is better thought of as the planning layer before execution. Its project management templates cover roadmaps, RACI, stakeholder maps, sprint rituals, project status, and PI planning, and the community library adds a lot of practical variations. That makes it especially useful when you need a kickoff that gets people on the same page before the work moves into a task tracker. For agencies, Miro is strong in workshops, scoping sessions, and client alignment meetings. Voting, timers, and facilitation features make it easier to run a structured discussion instead of an open-ended whiteboard session. When the team leaves with a clear scope, ownership map, and rough sequence, the handoff to Asana, Jira, monday.com, or another task tool is much cleaner. Use Miro to decide the work, then move the work into a system that actually tracks execution. The limit is simple. Miro is not a task system. If you try to execute everything inside it, your team will end up with planning boards that never become delivery boards. It works best when you treat it as the front end of the process, not the whole process. 9. TeamGantt TeamGantt is the clearest pick when the timeline matters more than anything else. Its Gantt chart templates cover construction, creative work, product and software, marketing, and events, so it fits agencies that need client-facing schedules with dependencies built in. If your clients ask for dates, milestones, and sequencing before they ask for anything else, this tool makes sense. The appeal is speed and clarity. You can save any project as a reusable template, which helps standardize recurring delivery types without rebuilding the schedule structure each time. It's also easy to explain to clients, which matters when you need a schedule that both your team and the client can read without a training session. The trade-off is scope. TeamGantt does scheduling well, but it doesn't try to be a full work OS. That keeps it focused, but it also means reporting and resource management feel lighter than enterprise suites. For teams where timing is the main issue, that's usually enough. If you're weighing a timeline-first setup against another chart style, the comparison in Gantt vs PERT chart can help keep the choice grounded in execution, not theory. 10. Microsoft Project A client signs off on the schedule, then asks for the same plan in a format the finance lead can track. Another stakeholder wants task ownership, dependencies, and cost rollups without learning a new system. Microsoft Project fits that kind of environment, especially in agencies and professional services firms that already standardize on Microsoft 365. The Microsoft templates and downloads cover project plans across Project, Excel, and Word, so the team can build schedules, WBS documents, dependencies, and cost tracking inside a familiar stack. That matters when the goal is not just to create a plan, but to keep the plan aligned with billing, status reporting, and client reviews. If your delivery process depends on structured artifacts, Microsoft Project gives you a format that seasoned PMs recognize immediately. Why teams still use it Traditional PM structure: It handles WBS, dependencies, and schedule logic cleanly, which helps when work needs to move from scoping into formal delivery. Microsoft stack fit: It works well for teams already using Excel, Word, and Project, so templates can be shared without creating a separate operating model. Template discipline: New projects start with a defined structure instead of a blank file, which helps standardize recurring engagements and reduce setup drift. Learning curve trade-off: The interface asks for more setup than lighter task tools, and the stronger features usually sit in higher plans. That is acceptable for teams that need detailed planning artifacts and already have people who know the Microsoft environment. For agencies that want to turn a template into a repeatable operating process, the plan usually needs one more layer. Standardize the schedule, map tasks to billing codes, and connect status updates to reporting so the template does more than store dates. A practical project management work plan gives a useful structure for that handoff, especially when the team needs the plan to stay useful after kickoff. For agencies and professional services firms, that link matters most when reporting and billing have to stay clean without adding more manual admin. That's where calendar-based tracking helps. TimeTackle can capture activity from Google or Outlook calendars, then turn that into a view of project time, utilization, and resource use without making people live in timesheets all day. It also fits this topic well because it pairs naturally with template-based planning. You can keep the project structure in your PM tool, then use calendar data to see whether the team followed the plan. One practical pattern is to keep a small template stack for charter, scope, RACI, status, and schedule, then map those artifacts to a reporting rhythm that comes from the calendar. That gives leaders better visibility and cuts duplicate reporting work, which is often where mid-sized agencies lose time. If your team is still jumping between a plan, a spreadsheet, and a timesheet system, the workflow is doing too much copying and not enough managing. title: Pony.ai Reports Record Growth in Paid Robotaxi Services; Joint Deployment Model to Accelerate Dual-Engine Expansion
summary: Robotaxi accounts for one-third of total revenue for the first time, with fare-charging revenue up 849.3% year-over-year Cost reductions, operational efficiency gains and improvements in rider experience delivered by Pony.ai’s seventh-generation (Gen-7) Robotaxis are supporting growth both in China and overseas.
body_text: Robotaxi accounts for one-third of total revenue for the first time, with fare-charging revenue up 849.3% year-over-year Cost reductions, operational efficiency gains and improvements in rider experience delivered by Pony.ai’s seventh-generation (Gen-7) Robotaxis are supporting growth both in China and overseas. This momentum puts the company on track to meet its full-year target of growing Robotaxi revenue to more than 3.5 times its 2025 level. According to its latest quarterly results, Pony.ai posted its strongest growth since it began separately reporting Robotaxi paid-service revenue. Fare-charging revenue surged 849.3% year-over-year in the second quarter, while total Robotaxi revenue increased 691.2% to US$12.1 million. Supported by the growth of its Robotaxi business, Pony.ai’s total revenue rose 68.8% year-over-year to US$36.2 million in the second quarter. Robotaxi accounted for one-third of total revenue for the first time , becoming an increasingly important contributor to the company’s growth. Pony.ai’s operating track record in China is also supporting its overseas expansion. Recent partnership agreements, including one with global mobility platform Uber , have expanded the company’s planned and potential overseas deployments to more than 4,000 Robotaxis , giving its joint deployment model greater commercial scale. Scaling a Proven Model in China Growth in Pony.ai’s home market was broad-based, supported by solid operational execution and an improved rider experience across a growing range of everyday mobility needs. The company’s number of registered users in China reached 1.5 million. In Guangzhou, where Pony.ai has achieved unit economics breakeven, operations expanded beyond Nansha District into central urban areas including Haizhu, Tianhe, Huangpu and Panyu. The expansion has added around 300 square kilometers of operational coverage since the beginning of the year, serving more than 7 million people across areas that include major tourist attractions, business districts and clusters of corporate headquarters. In neighboring Shenzhen, where Pony.ai has also reached unit economics breakeven, its Robotaxis now serve several of the city’s most important transportation gateways, connecting the network with high-volume air, sea and cross-border travel. These include Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport, Shekou Cruise Homeport—a major cruise and ferry terminal—and Shenzhen Bay Port, a major land crossing with Hong Kong where daily passenger traffic reached a record 215,000 earlier this year. Following the commercial rollout of two Gen-7 Robotaxi models, a third model developed and manufactured in partnership with Toyota also entered service in China’s tier-one cities. The additional model is supporting greater deployment density and a more consistent ride-hailing experience. Pony.ai’s total Robotaxi fleet reached 1,975 vehicles as of June 30, 2026. Building Global Scale Through Joint Deployment As scaled Gen-7 deployment begins translating into stronger commercial results in China, Pony.ai’s overseas business is also gaining momentum. The operating track record built in its home market—spanning fully driverless service, sustained rider demand and positive unit economics—is providing partners with a tested foundation for deployment in new markets. The company recently secured multiple partnerships under the joint deployment model, bringing its total overseas deployment pipeline to over 4,000 vehicles. Among the partnerships, Pony.ai and Uber plan to deploy more than 2,000 Pony.ai Robotaxis in Europe. Pony.ai’s joint deployment model brings together the three core capabilities required to scale Robotaxi services: autonomous driving technology, access to rider demand and day-to-day fleet operations. Pony.ai provides its L4 technology and commercialization experience; mobility platforms connect services with users and support functions such as booking, payment and customer service; and local operating partners manage vehicle deployment and fleet operations. The mix of partners can vary by market, allowing the model to adapt to local requirements while supporting a more capital-efficient path to scale. Pony.ai also made progress in Singapore and Luxembourg during the second quarter. In Singapore, Pony.ai and ComfortDelGro made their autonomous mobility service in Punggol available for booking through ComfortDelGro’s Zig app, expanding access beyond the earlier by-invite phase. In Luxembourg, Pony.ai, Bolt and Stellantis launched an autonomous mobility pilot to validate safety, performance and regulatory readiness in local traffic conditions, with the partners working toward fully driverless readiness by the end of the program. Dr. Tiancheng Lou, Founder and CTO of Pony.ai , commented, “Our strategic early investments in full-stack L4 autonomous technology and advanced world models are now translating into greater efficiency across research and development, testing and fleet operations. PonyWorld 2.0 enables us to deploy Robotaxi fleets across multiple countries and cities simultaneously without a proportionate increase in engineering resources. ” Robotruck Revenue Rises as Gen-4 Deliveries Begin Pony.ai’s Robotruck business also delivered strong results in the second quarter, with revenue increasing 40% year-over-year. The company has begun mass production of its fourth-generation (Gen-4) Robotrucks on schedule and has initiated commercial deliveries. Pony.ai partnered with China Merchants Port in Shenzhen to begin commercial deployment of Gen-4 driverless Robotrucks in real-world, mixed-fleet logistics operations. During the second quarter, the company’s Intelligent Solutions business recorded revenue of US$10.8 million, broadly flat from the same period last year. Net loss in the second quarter narrowed 14.9% year-over-year to US$45.4 million, primarily due to certain non-operating items. “Our progress across China and international markets shows that autonomous driving at scale is not only technologically viable, but increasingly commercially sustainable, with a clearer path to profitability,” said Dr. Leo Wang, Co-founder and CFO of Pony.ai. “We have the momentum and financial resources to execute against our full-year priorities while continuing to invest for sustained, multi-year growth.” About Pony AI Inc. Pony AI Inc. is a global leader in achieving large-scale commercialization of autonomous mobility. Leveraging its vehicle-agnostic Virtual Driver technology, a full-stack autonomous driving technology that seamlessly integrates Pony.ai's proprietary software, hardware and services, Pony.ai is developing a commercially viable and sustainable business model that enables the mass production and deployment of vehicles across transportation use cases. Founded in 2016, Pony.ai has expanded its presence across China, Europe, Asia, the Middle East and other regions, ensuring widespread access to its advanced technology.
